title: The Word About Words
subtitle: Aphorisms on language from the Great Conversation
author: Tristan

sections.name: Hebrew Bible
sections.intro: In Genesis, speech creates, naming confers identity, and a shared language is power. Dates are the conventional range for the composition of the text (roughly 10th–5th centuries BCE). Hebrew from the Masoretic Text; English KJV.

sections.name: New Testament
sections.intro: The Greek Logos runs from John's prologue to the last chapter of Revelation, where the book seals its own text. Koine Greek; English KJV; links go to Bible Hub's Greek–English interlinear.

sections.name: Homer
sections.intro: Homer gives the West its first word-trick, a name that means "Nobody." Homeric Greek, Monro–Allen text; Iliad c. 750–700 BCE, Odyssey c. 725–675 BCE. Links go to the Perseus Scaife reader.

sections.name: Presocratics and Sophists
sections.intro: The first surviving sentence of Western philosophy already describes the cosmos in borrowed legal language. Fragments are cited by Diels–Kranz (DK) number; dates are approximate floruits. Greek text: Diels, *Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker*, Greek–German, 1906, [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/diefragmentederv01diel/page/2/mode/2up).

sections.name: Thucydides
sections.intro: Thucydides is the first writer to describe how civil war corrupts the meaning of words, 2,300 years before Orwell. *History of the Peloponnesian War*, written c. 431–400 BCE; Greek text of H. S. Jones (Oxford, 1910). Thomas Hobbes made the first English translation from the Greek, in 1629.

sections.name: Plato and Aristotle
sections.intro: Plato asks whether names are natural and warns that writing breeds forgetting; Aristotle answers that names are conventional signs. Plato cited by Stephanus page (Burnet's Greek text); Aristotle by Bekker page.

sections.name: Rome
sections.intro: Lucretius argues that names grew from need, not from a single name-giver, and builds his atomism on an analogy with letters. Horace makes usage the judge of words. Latin text; my translations.

sections.name: India: Pāṇini
sections.intro: Pāṇini's *Aṣṭādhyāyī* ("Eight Chapters," c. 4th century BCE) generates the whole of Sanskrit from about 4,000 terse rules (*sūtra*), run on a small alphabet of markers and technical terms. It has meta-rules for applying rules, a mechanism for abbreviating sets of sounds, and a policy for resolving rule conflicts. It is the oldest surviving formal grammar, and arguably the oldest surviving program. Sanskrit in Devanagari with transliteration; my translations. [Text and commentary, ashtadhyayi.com](https://ashtadhyayi.com/)

sections.name: India: the Bhagavad Gita
sections.intro: In the Gita, God names himself as a syllable, a letter, and a grammatical form, and the Sanskrit word for "letter," *akṣara*, also means "imperishable." Composed c. 2nd century BCE–2nd century CE as part of the *Mahābhārata*. Sanskrit in Devanagari; my translations. [English, Edwin Arnold, *The Song Celestial* (1885), Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2388)

sections.name: Late antiquity and Middle Ages
sections.intro: Augustine defines the sign, Boethius wears letters, the Beowulf poet unlocks a word-hoard, and Aquinas ends by calling his own words straw.

sections.name: Arabic and Persian
sections.intro: The Baghdad translation movement made language itself a problem: can Greek logic be thought in Arabic, and can mathematics be written in words alone? Where I could not confirm the original wording, the entry gives the Arabic or Persian title and paraphrases the argument.

sections.name: Renaissance
sections.intro: Machiavelli sees that a new religion conquers by changing the language, and that a reformer keeps the old names while changing the substance. Montaigne, Shakespeare and Bacon turn suspicion of words into an art.

sections.name: Seventeenth century
sections.intro: Descartes makes language the test of a mind; Hobbes and Locke make words the currency, and the fog, of thought.

sections.name: Eighteenth century
sections.intro: The Enlightenment argues about where language came from (passion, need, or human nature itself) and begins to suspect that thinking is a kind of talking.

sections.name: Nineteenth century
sections.intro: The Romantics call language fossil poetry; Kierkegaard says the poet pays for the power of words with one secret he cannot tell; Carroll and Nietzsche show that words can be made to mean anything.

sections.name: Early twentieth century
sections.intro: Saussure makes meaning a system of differences; Hofmannsthal watches words rot; Wittgenstein draws the limits of language and then dissolves them. Wittgenstein's *Investigations* and Heidegger are in copyright, so those quotations are kept short.

sections.name: Mid twentieth century
sections.intro: Two Oxford philologists make language the root of myth; Orwell makes it the root of tyranny; Quine doubts there is a fact of the matter about meaning at all. All are in copyright: short quotations, the rest paraphrased, with publishers named.

sections.name: Late twentieth century
sections.intro: Derrida finds nothing outside the text; Foucault finds that "man" is a recent arrangement of words; Philip K. Dick suspects the Word is alive. All in copyright: short quotations, publishers named.

sections.name: Media and the medium
sections.intro: Plato feared that writing would hollow out memory; two millennia later a group of scholars, most of them in Toronto, asked what each new medium does to the minds that use it. Innis finds that media tilt empires toward time or space; Havelock reads Plato's war on the poets as literacy's war on oral memory; McLuhan declares that the medium, not the content, is the message; Ong shows that writing restructures consciousness; Postman applies all of it to television. All in copyright: short quotations, publishers named.

sections.name: Machines and grammars
sections.intro: Chomsky gives grammar a mathematics; Backus and Naur turn it into the notation in which programming languages are defined; Dijkstra insists that formal language is a privilege and natural language a trap; Naur ends by locating the program not in the text at all but in the programmers' heads. All in copyright except where Dijkstra's manuscripts are freely posted: short quotations, sources named.

sections.name: Physicists
sections.intro: Einstein marks the gap between mathematics and reality and says he does not think in words; Heisenberg makes a word's meaning depend on the experiment that measures it, and records Bohr saying that about atoms language can only be poetry; Hawking asks what breathes fire into the equations. German from the original publications where they exist; English translations the editor's own unless named. All in copyright: short quotations, sources named.

sections.name: Star Trek
sections.intro: Star Trek assumes a universal translator and then, in its best episode on language, shows why translating every word still leaves you understanding nothing. Episodes and films are in copyright; short quotations only. The series and films stream on Paramount+ and are sold on disc.

sections.name: Neal Stephenson
sections.intro: Stephenson writes novels in which language is code: a virus in Sumerian, a philosophy with its own invented lexicon, a worm named for the file you are told to read first. In copyright; paraphrase and short quotations only.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Cosmic order is put in legal words: dikē[justice; penalty] and tisis[retribution]. Nietzsche (*Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks*, 1873) and Heidegger ("Der Spruch des Anaximander," 1946) both wrote essays on this one sentence.

place.name: Magna Graecia (Elea?)
place.why: wandering Sicily and south Italy after leaving Colophon

quotes.orig: ἀλλ᾽ εἰ χεῖρας ἔχον βόες ἵπποι τ᾽ ἠὲ λέοντες / ἢ γράψαι χείρεσσι καὶ ἔργα τελεῖν ἅπερ ἄνδρες, / ἵπποι μέν θ᾽ ἵπποισι, βόες δέ τε βουσὶν ὁμοίας / καί κε θεῶν ἰδέας ἔγραφον…
quotes.translit: all' ei cheiras echon boes hippoi t' ēe leontes / ē grapsai cheiressi kai erga telein haper andres, / hippoi men th' hippoisi, boes de te bousin homoias / kai ke theōn ideas egraphon…

entries.author: gorgias
entries.date_note: date very uncertain; late 5th c. BCE

place.name: Athens?
place.why: itinerant sophist active in Athens after 427

entries.context: Gorgias defends Helen: if speech persuaded her, she is not to blame.

quotes.orig: λόγος δυνάστης μέγας ἐστίν, ὃς σμικροτάτῳ σώματι καὶ ἀφανεστάτῳ θειότατα ἔργα ἀποτελεῖ.
quotes.translit: logos dynastēs megas estin, hos smikrotatōi sōmati kai aphanestatōi theiotata erga apotelei.
quotes.trans: Speech is a mighty lord, who with the smallest and most invisible body accomplishes the most divine works.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Speech is a dynastēs[lord, ruler]. Gorgias goes on to compare speech's effect on the soul to a drug's effect on the body.

entries.author: thucydides

place.name: Thrace (exile)
place.why: likely written during exile after 424 BCE

entries.context: In his statement of method, Thucydides explains how he rendered the speeches in his history.

quotes.orig: ὡς δ᾽ ἂν ἐδόκουν μοι ἕκαστοι περὶ τῶν αἰεὶ παρόντων τὰ δέοντα μάλιστ᾽ εἰπεῖν
quotes.translit: hōs d' an edokoun moi hekastoi peri tōn aiei parontōn ta deonta malist' eipein
quotes.trans: As it seemed to me each speaker would most likely have said what the occasion required.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Thucydides admits his famous speeches are reconstructions.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: thucydides

place.name: Thrace (exile)
place.why: likely written during exile after 424 BCE

entries.context: Thucydides explains why his history may seem less pleasing to listeners.

quotes.orig: κτῆμά τε ἐς αἰεὶ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀγώνισμα ἐς τὸ παραχρῆμα ἀκούειν ξύγκειται.
quotes.translit: ktēma te es aiei mallon ē agōnisma es to parachrēma akouein xynkeitai.
quotes.trans: It is composed as a possession for all time, rather than a prize-piece to be heard for the moment.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Writing set against oral performance: a ktēma[possession] for all time, not an agōnisma[prize-piece].

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: thucydides
entries.date_note: oration delivered winter 431/430 BCE; written up later

place.name: Athens
place.why: Thucydides was in Athens when Pericles spoke

entries.context: Pericles' Funeral Oration praises Athenian democracy.

quotes.orig: οὐ τοὺς λόγους τοῖς ἔργοις βλάβην ἡγούμενοι
quotes.translit: ou tous logous tois ergois blabēn hēgoumenoi
quotes.trans: We do not think that words are a hindrance to deeds.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Athens defines itself as a city that talks before it acts: logos[word] with ergon[deed].

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: thucydides
entries.date_note: events of 427 BCE; written c. 424–400 BCE

place.name: Thrace (exile)
place.why: likely written during exile after 424 BCE

entries.context: During the civil war in Corcyra, Thucydides describes how faction corrupted the city.

quotes.orig: καὶ τὴν εἰωθυῖαν ἀξίωσιν τῶν ὀνομάτων ἐς τὰ ἔργα ἀντήλλαξαν τῇ δικαιώσει. τόλμα μὲν γὰρ ἀλόγιστος ἀνδρεία φιλέταιρος ἐνομίσθη, μέλλησις δὲ προμηθὴς δειλία εὐπρεπής, τὸ δὲ σῶφρον τοῦ ἀνάνδρου πρόσχημα.
quotes.translit: kai tēn eiōthuian axiōsin tōn onomatōn es ta erga antēllaxan tēi dikaiōsei. tolma men gar alogistos andreia philetairos enomisthē, mellēsis de promēthēs deilia euprepēs, to de sōphron tou anandrou proschēma.
quotes.trans: They changed the customary meaning of words in relation to deeds, as they saw fit. Reckless daring came to be considered loyal courage; prudent hesitation, specious cowardice; moderation, a cloak for unmanliness.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: When politics breaks down, the meanings of words shift first.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: socrates

place.name: Athens
place.why: lived and taught in Athens

entries.context: Socrates left no writings. He is known only through others: Plato's dialogues, Xenophon's memoirs, and Aristophanes' mockery in the Clouds (423 BCE). The three portraits disagree.
entries.interpretation: Placeholder: The founder of Western philosophy is a character in other people's books. Separating the historical man from Plato's spokesman is the "Socratic problem": the critic of writing survives only as writing, and the speaker behind the text cannot be recovered.

source.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Socrates"

entries.author: plato

place.name: Athens (Academy)
place.why: teaching at the newly founded Academy

entries.context: Hermogenes reports Cratylus' thesis, which Socrates spends the dialogue testing against Hermogenes' view that names are mere convention.

quotes.orig: ὀνόματος ὀρθότητα εἶναι ἑκάστῳ τῶν ὄντων φύσει πεφυκυῖαν
quotes.translit: onomatos orthotēta einai hekastōi tōn ontōn physei pephykuian
quotes.trans: There is a correctness of name for each thing, belonging to it by nature.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Are names correct by physis[nature] or by agreement? The founding question of the philosophy of language.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: plato

place.name: Athens (Academy)
place.why: Academy period between Sicilian voyages

entries.context: King Thamus answers the god Theuth, who offers writing as a gift to Egypt.

quotes.orig: τοῦτο γὰρ τῶν μαθόντων λήθην μὲν ἐν ψυχαῖς παρέξει μνήμης ἀμελετησίᾳ… οὔκουν μνήμης ἀλλὰ ὑπομνήσεως φάρμακον ηὗρες.
quotes.translit: touto gar tōn mathontōn lēthēn men en psychais parexei mnēmēs ameletēsiāi… oukoun mnēmēs alla hypomnēseōs pharmakon hēures.
quotes.trans: This will produce forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn it, through neglect of memory… You have found a drug not for memory but for reminding.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Derrida's essay "Plato's Pharmacy" (1968) is built on the word *pharmakon*[remedy and poison], which means both remedy and poison.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: plato

place.name: Athens (Academy)
place.why: Academy period between Sicilian voyages

entries.context: Socrates continues his critique of writing after the myth of Theuth.

quotes.orig: ἐὰν δ᾽ ἀνέρῃ τι, σεμνῶς πάνυ σιγᾷ.
quotes.translit: ean d' anerēi ti, semnōs pany sigāi.
quotes.trans: if you ask them something, they keep a most solemn silence.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Written words are like paintings: "if you ask them something, they keep a most solemn silence."

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: plato

place.name: Athens (Academy)
place.why: Academy period between Sicilian voyages

entries.context: Socrates finishes his complaint against written words: once written, a text drifts everywhere, reaching those who understand it and those who don't.

quotes.orig: τοῦ πατρὸς ἀεὶ δεῖται βοηθοῦ
quotes.translit: tou patros aei deitai boēthou
quotes.trans: it always needs its father to help it

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: A text cannot defend itself or answer questions; without its author it is an orphan. Every documentation problem since.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: plato

place.name: Athens (Academy)
place.why: Academy period between Sicilian voyages

entries.context: Socrates describes a better kind of word, one written in the soul of the learner, and Phaedrus names it.

quotes.orig: τὸν τοῦ εἰδότος λόγον λέγεις ζῶντα καὶ ἔμψυχον, οὗ ὁ γεγραμμένος εἴδωλον ἄν τι λέγοιτο δικαίως.
quotes.translit: ton tou eidotos logon legeis zōnta kai empsychon, hou ho gegrammenos eidōlon an ti legoito dikaiōs.
quotes.trans: You mean the living and ensouled word of the one who knows, of which the written word might fairly be called an image.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: The written word is an eidōlon[image, phantom] of the living one. The paradox, which Derrida exploits, is that Plato makes the case in writing, and the only Socrates we have is a written one. Naur's "theory" that lives in programmers rather than in code is the same claim.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: plato

place.name: Athens (Academy)
place.why: back in Athens after the last Sicilian voyage

entries.context: Plato rebukes those who have written about his teachings on the highest mathēma[subject of study].

quotes.orig: ῥητὸν γὰρ οὐδαμῶς ἐστιν ὡς ἄλλα μαθήματα… ἐξαίφνης, οἷον ἀπὸ πυρὸς πηδήσαντος ἐξαφθὲν φῶς, ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ γενόμενον
quotes.translit: rhēton gar oudamōs estin hōs alla mathēmata… exaiphnēs, hoion apo pyros pēdēsantos exaphthen phōs, en tēi psychēi genomenon
quotes.trans: It cannot be put into words like other studies… but suddenly, like light kindled from a leaping spark, it is born in the soul.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Plato's own Tractatus[Wittgenstein's treatise] 7: what matters most cannot be said.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: aristotle

place.name: Athens (Academy)
place.why: logical works usually placed in the Academy years

entries.context: Aristotle opens his treatise on propositions by defining spoken and written words.

quotes.orig: Ἔστι μὲν οὖν τὰ ἐν τῇ φωνῇ τῶν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ παθημάτων σύμβολα, καὶ τὰ γραφόμενα τῶν ἐν τῇ φωνῇ.
quotes.translit: Esti men oun ta en tēi phōnēi tōn en tēi psychēi pathēmatōn symbola, kai ta graphomena tōn en tēi phōnēi.
quotes.trans: Spoken sounds are symbols of affections in the soul, and written marks are symbols of spoken sounds.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: The foundation of Western semantics for two thousand years: words as symbola[tokens, signs] of pathēmata[affections] in the soul.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: aristotle

place.name: Athens (Academy)
place.why: logical works usually placed in the Academy years

entries.context: Aristotle defines the onoma[name, noun] at the start of his analysis.

quotes.orig: Ὄνομα μὲν οὖν ἐστὶ φωνὴ σημαντικὴ κατὰ συνθήκην
quotes.translit: Onoma men oun esti phōnē sēmantikē kata synthēkēn
quotes.trans: A name is a sound significant by convention.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Aristotle's answer to the *Cratylus*: names hold by synthēkē[convention].

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: lucretius

place.name: Rome
place.why: presumed Roman; poem dedicated to Memmius

entries.context: Lucretius argues that nothing comes from nothing and that things share atoms.

quotes.orig: ut potius multis communia corpora rebus / multa putes esse, ut verbis elementa videmus, / quam sine principiis ullam rem exsistere posse.
quotes.trans: Rather believe that many bodies are common to many things, as we see letters common to words, than that anything can exist without first-beginnings.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: *Elementa*[letters; atoms] means both "letters" and "atoms": the universe is spelled. He returns to the analogy at 1.823–827 and 2.688–699.

source.label: English, Leonard 1916

entries.author: lucretius

place.name: Rome
place.why: presumed Roman; poem dedicated to Memmius

entries.context: In his history of civilization, Lucretius turns to the origin of language.

quotes.orig: at varios linguae sonitus natura subegit / mittere et utilitas expressit nomina rerum.
quotes.trans: But nature drove men to utter the various sounds of the tongue, and usefulness pressed out the names of things.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Language arose from nature and utilitas[usefulness, need], not invention.

source.label: English, Leonard 1916

entries.author: lucretius

place.name: Rome
place.why: presumed Roman; poem dedicated to Memmius

entries.context: Lucretius continues his account of how language arose.

quotes.orig: proinde putare aliquem tum nomina distribuisse / rebus et inde homines didicisse vocabula prima, / desiperest.
quotes.trans: To think that someone back then handed out names to things, and that men learned their first words from him, is madness.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: A direct rejection of a single original name-giver, whether Adam in Genesis 2:19 or the lawgiver of the *Cratylus*.

source.label: English, Leonard 1916

entries.author: horace

place.name: Rome
place.why: late career in Rome and Sabine farm

entries.context: Horace advises a young poet on choosing words.

quotes.orig: dixeris egregie, notum si callida verbum / reddiderit iunctura novum.
quotes.trans: You will speak exceptionally well if a clever combination makes a familiar word new.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Novelty lies in the iunctura[joining of words], not in new words.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: horace

place.name: Rome
place.why: late career in Rome and Sabine farm

entries.context: Horace on how vocabulary rises and falls over time.

quotes.orig: multa renascentur quae iam cecidere, cadentque / quae nunc sunt in honore vocabula, si volet usus, / quem penes arbitrium est et ius et norma loquendi.
quotes.trans: Many words now fallen will be reborn, and many now honored will fall, if usage wills it, in whose hands lie the judgment, the law, and the rule of speaking.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Two millennia before Wittgenstein, usus[usage] is the authority.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: horace

place.name: Rome
place.why: late career in Rome and Sabine farm

entries.context: Horace advises keeping a poem nine years before publishing.

quotes.orig: delere licebit / quod non edideris; nescit vox missa reverti.
quotes.trans: What you have not published you may destroy; the word once sent forth cannot return.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Publication is irreversible: a word sent out cannot be recalled.

source.label: Perseus

entries.author: horace

place.name: Rome
place.why: late career in Rome and Sabine farm

entries.context: Horace advises a young friend on discretion with powerful patrons.

quotes.orig: et semel emissum volat irrevocabile verbum.
quotes.trans: And a word once let out flies, beyond recall.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: A spoken word cannot be unsaid.

source.label: Horace, Epistulae 1.18.71 (The Latin Library text)

entries.author: latin-proverb
entries.date_note: medieval; no dated attestation located, c. 1300 chosen

place.name: Latin Europe
place.why: origin unknown; placed nominally at Rome

entries.context: A medieval Latin proverb, often attributed to a speech in the Roman Senate.

quotes.orig: Verba volant, scripta manent.
quotes.trans: Spoken words fly away; written ones remain.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Speech is fleeting, writing endures; the line has been read as both praise and warning.

entries.author: caesar

place.name: Gaul (winter quarters, Bibracte?)
place.why: composed in Gaul between campaigns

entries.context: Caesar describes the Druids of Gaul, whose pupils spend up to twenty years memorizing verse. The Druids use Greek letters for everyday records but refuse to write their teachings down, for two reasons: so the doctrine does not reach the common people, and so learners do not neglect memory.

quotes.orig: …quod fere plerisque accidit ut praesidio litterarum diligentiam in perdiscendo ac memoriam remittant.
quotes.trans: …which happens to most people: trusting to the protection of letters, they relax their effort in learning and their memory.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: Plato's warning about writing, observed in a living oral culture three centuries later, and combined with a second motive, secrecy. Writing both spreads knowledge and weakens the memory that held it.

source.label: The Latin Library

quotes.translit: a i u ṇ
quotes.trans: a i u ṇ.

place.name: Śalātura, near Gandhāra

quotes.translit: ādir antyena sahetā

entries.author: panini

place.name: Śalātura, near Gandhāra
place.why: traditional birthplace; date conventional

quotes.translit: vṛddhir ādaic
quotes.trans: Vṛddhi[strongest vowel grade] (is the name for) ā, ai, au.

source.label: Text and commentary, ashtadhyayi.com

entries.author: panini

place.name: Śalātura, near Gandhāra
place.why: traditional birthplace; date conventional

entries.context: A rule telling the reader how to read words cited inside the grammar's own rules.

quotes.orig: स्वं रूपं शब्दस्याशब्दसंज्ञा
quotes.translit: svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasyāśabdasaṃjñā
quotes.trans: A word (in a rule) stands for its own form, except when it is a technical term.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: This is the distinction between using a word and mentioning it, stated about 2,300 years before logicians named it.

source.label: Text and commentary, ashtadhyayi.com

entries.author: panini

place.name: Śalātura, near Gandhāra
place.why: traditional birthplace; date conventional

quotes.orig: विप्रतिषेधे परं कार्यम्
quotes.translit: vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam
quotes.trans: When (two rules) conflict, the later one applies.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: The commentators spent two millennia arguing about what "later" means.

entries.author: nagesha
entries.date_note: early 18th century; a maxim of the grammarians

place.name: Varanasi
place.why: Nāgeśa worked in Varanasi

quotes.translit: ardhamātrālāghavena putrotsavaṃ manyante vaiyākaraṇāḥ
quotes.trans: Grammarians rejoice over saving half a mora[syllable length unit] as over the birth of a son.

entries.interpretation: Placeholder: The tradition's own joke about its love of brevity.
